notes:
I've written notes on Galatians 4 below, taken only from pages I could open or see in search results.

**Gaps:**
- I couldn't reach any Wesleyan/Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed), Pentecostal-specific (ag.org, pneumareview, samstorms), or LCMS/1517 pages.
- I found no NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey, catholic.com or oca.org pages on this chapter.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so that section is left out.
- Gill's notes appeared only for vv. 10 and 24.
- The church tradition given for each author (e.g. "Baptist") is my own label. The pages don't state it.

## Verses 1–3
- **v. 1 (child = minor):** Both the child and the slave were incapable of any valid act in a legal sense; the guardian was as entirely the representative of the one as the master of the other. Both the child and the slave were subject to the same restraint (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 1:** Guzik: the young heir has less day-to-day freedom than a high-ranking household slave, yet, he is *destined* to inherit everything and the slave isn't. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 1 (Old Testament church):** Matthew Henry says the Old Testament church was like a child under age, kept in comparative darkness and bondage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm
- **v. 2:** Ellicott says the two words mean guardians of the person and stewards of the property. Neither Greek nor Roman law let the father set the length of minority, so Paul's application (God fixes humanity's minority) has shaped the illustration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 2:** Guzik thinks the phrase "time appointed by the father" fits the Roman coming-of-age custom best. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 3 ("we"):** Ellicott: "we" means first the Jews, but Gentiles are included too. Before Christ, both were under law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 3 ("elements") – a real debate:**
  - Ellicott notes that most older commentators took "elements" as the heavenly bodies. He prefers "rudiments of religious teaching", which were earthly and material and centred on ritual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says that because the Law was God's own ordinance, the phrase marks the qualification of imperfection and inferiority, not moral evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/galatians/4.htm
  - Guzik, following Barclay and Cole, calls it the "ABC of the universe": the cause-and-effect, earn-and-deserve principle found in paganism as well as in law. Grace contradicts it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
  - Some modern translations read "elemental spirits" in v. 9 (NRSV, CJB). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/galatians/4-10.html

## Verses 4–5
- **v. 4 ("fullness of time"):** Ellicott says this matches "the time appointed of the father" in v. 2. It shows religion as progressive, reaching its high point in Christianity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/galatians-4.html
- **v. 4:** MacLaren grants that the world was prepared (Jewish law, decaying paganism, Roman roads). But Paul is not thinking of the fulness of time primarily in reference to the world which received Him, but to the Father who sent Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/4-4.htm
- **v. 4:** Guzik also points to Daniel's prophesied 483 years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 4 ("sent forth"):** Ellicott says this shows the Son already existed before he was born. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 4 ("born of a woman") – the Virgin Birth is disputed:**
  - Ellicott (Anglican): There is no allusion here to the miraculous conception. The phrase stresses Christ's true humanity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/galatians-4.html
  - Guzik says it may be a veiled reference to the Virgin Birth, and quotes Luther saying Paul obviously has the virgin in mind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
  - But Luther's commentary as given on StudyLight says Paul is now treating of faith and Christian righteousness, of the person and office of Christ, not of the virginity of Mary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
- **v. 4 ("under the law") – Lutheran emphasis:** Luther says Christ voluntarily let the Law accuse and condemn him. He was not an agent of the Law but a patient of the Law. He was not a law-giver, but a law-taker. Luther sets this against the "Roman" view of Christ as a stricter lawgiver. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
- **v. 4:** Matthew Henry: "made of a woman" is the incarnation, and "made under the law" is his subjection to it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm
- **v. 5 (redeem, then adopt):**
  - Ellicott: Christ ransomed both Jew and Gentile at the price of his death, and Redemption is followed by adoption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - MacLaren: the order matters, since there must be redemption from law before there is the adoption of sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/4-4.htm
- **v. 5:** Luther says God adopted us because of the merit of Christ, who humbled himself under the Law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
- **v. 5:** Guzik: we receive adoption rather than recover it. Adam was never adopted the way believers are, so we get more in Jesus than Adam had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 5 (Orthodox/Catholic):** Chrysostom names two results of the Incarnation: deliverance from the curse of the Law, and promotion to sonship. He says "receive" implies something owed, because it was promised to Abraham. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm

## Verses 6–7
- **v. 6 ("because" – does sonship come before the Spirit?):**
  - Ellicott keeps "because" but says it could mean "in proof that". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary: God sent the Spirit because believers had already received adoption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/galatians/4.htm
  - Chrysostom: Had not we been first made sons, we could not have called Him Father. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 6 (assurance):**
  - Calvin (quoted by Guzik) says "crying" expresses certainty and confidence.
  - Stott (quoted by Guzik): the Son gives the status of sonship, and the Spirit gives the experience of it.
  - Guzik links the verse to Romans 8:16 and notes the Trinity in the verse.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 6 ("Abba" as "Daddy"):** Guzik reports a dispute. Cole calls "Daddy" over-sentimental. Boice says the Antiochene Fathers agree that "Abba" was a small child's word for its father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 6:** Matthew Henry: everyone who is adopted has the Spirit of adoption, which is always the Spirit of prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm
- **v. 7:**
  - Ellicott: the singular "you" makes the point personal to each reader.
  - The better Greek reading may be "heir through God".
  - Roman law treated all sons as equal heirs.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 7:** Guzik: We inherit **God** Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/

## Verses 8–11
- **v. 8:**
  - Ellicott ties "not gods" to 1 Corinthians 10:20, where Paul calls the pagan gods demons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - Matthew Henry: worship belongs only to the one who is God by nature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm
  - The Pulpit Commentary: Paul is not excusing their idolatry but describing real guilt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 9 ("or rather are known by God"):**
  - Ellicott: this corrects any overstress on the human side. To be known by God means God recognises and accepts you. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - Chrysostom: It was not by your own pains that you found out God, but while you continued in error, He drew you to Himself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 9 ("weak and worthless"):** Ellicott: "weak" because they cannot save, and "beggarly" because, unlike the gospel, they brought no outpouring of the Spirit. "Again" means starting over, like a child going back to the alphabet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 9:** Guzik: the Galatians were going back to an old error, a works-based relationship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- **v. 10 (traditional reading):** Ellicott: days are the Sabbaths, months the new moons, seasons Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, and years the sabbatical year and jubilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 10 (Christian holy days – traditions differ):**
  - **Anglican (Ellicott):** It does not necessarily follow that the observance of Christian seasons is condemned. But such things are "rudiments", and Ellicott advises following the Church's general rule thoughtfully. He also cites Origen: for the mature Christian, every day is the Lord's Day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - **The Pulpit Commentary's homiletic notes** take a stricter view. They say the verse condemns the Church appointing permanent stated days, and allow only the Christian Sabbath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/galatians-4.html
  - **Reformed (Calvin):** No condemnation is here given to the observance of dates in the arrangements of civil society. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-10.html
  - **Baptist (Gill):** this is not about civil calendars but about ceremonies that pointed to Christ and are now fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/galatians/4-10.html
  - **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith)** applies the verse to Lent and All Saints' Day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-10.html
  - **Chrysostom** calls this rigid observance of days a kind of idolatry for Gentile believers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 11:** The Pulpit homiletics say that if this legalism was the only fruit, Paul would count his mission "love's labour lost". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/galatians/4.htm

## Verses 12–20
- **v. 12:** Ellicott: "become like me" means use the same Christian freedom I use. Paul set aside his Jewish privileges to stand level with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 12:** Chrysostom: after sharp rebuke, Paul softens and pours in encouragement "like oil". "You did me no wrong" shows he writes out of love, not ill will. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 12:** Luther: what changed their attitude toward Paul was false doctrine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
- **v. 13 (the illness – interpretations differ):**
  - Precept Austin suggests a long-standing eye problem, possibly the "thorn in the flesh". https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-4-commentary
  - The Pulpit homiletics lean the same way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/galatians/4.htm
  - Chrysostom instead reads it as persecution: I was driven about, I was scourged, I suffered a thousand deaths. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 14:** Chrysostom: having been received as an angel, how could Paul repay them with harm? https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 14:** Expositor's: far from being put off, they welcomed him with enthusiasm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 15:**
  - Expositor's: once they considered themselves blessed to have him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/galatians/4.htm
  - The Pulpit homiletics say the "eyes" remark may or may not point to an eye problem, but it certainly shows warm affection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 16:** Matthew Henry: people often treat their best friends as enemies, and ministers must not stop speaking the truth for fear of offending. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm
- **v. 17:** Ellicott: the word means to court or canvass someone. The Judaisers wanted to cut Galatia off from the other Gentile churches and make a sect by itself, in which they themselves may bear rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 18:** Chrysostom: the true blessing is to hold right views whether the teacher is present or not. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 19:**
  - W. E. Vine hears a reproach: has anyone heard of a mother giving birth to the same children twice? https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-4-commentary
  - Guzik: a pastor must aim to form Christ in people, not himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
  - Chrysostom: they have spoiled the likeness and need to be formed again, yet Paul still calls them children. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 20:** Chrysostom: "change my tone" means changing to tears, which a letter cannot carry. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 20:** Matthew Henry: Paul hoped to find things better than he feared. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_004.cfm

## Verses 21–31
- **v. 21:** Chrysostom: Paul now shows that the Law itself tells them to stop keeping it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **vv. 22–23:**
  - Ellicott: both sons were Abraham's, but one was born naturally, the other by divine instrumentality. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - TGC (Reformed): Ishmael was "according to the flesh" because Abraham and Sarah tried to produce the heir by their own efforts. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/galatians/
  - Chrysostom: Isaac came from a womb that was dead, formed by God's word, so being born "not after the flesh" is the greater honour. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- **v. 24 (what "allegory" means):**
  - Ellicott: the allegorical sense is added to the literal one and does not replace it. https://biblehub.com/galatians/4-24.htm
  - Constable: Paul was calling allegory what we refer to as analogy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-24.html
  - TGC: Paul combines this with a typological reading. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/galatians/
  - Chrysostom: Contrary to usage, he calls a type an allegory. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
  - Ellicott and Gill both note that Philo had already allegorised the story, very differently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/4-24.htm
- **v. 24 (scholarly view):** The ISBE entry on the Bible.org NET Bible site says the term may not be a technical method at all, or the passage may be an argumentum ad hominem (an argument aimed at his opponents' own terms). https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=allegory
- **v. 24 (which covenant is Hagar? – a split even among Baptists):**
  - Gill: Hagar is not the covenant of works, which was made in Eden with Adam. She is the Sinai covenant made only with Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-24.html
  - Spurgeon (on the same page) traces the Hagar covenant back to Eden.
  - Calvin (Reformed): the two mothers are two kinds of doctrine, legal and evangelical.
  - Matthew Henry: Sinai was a dispensation of grace, yet bondage compared with the gospel.
- **v. 24 (Piper, Baptist):** Piper doubts Genesis originally referred to Sinai, but sees the same truth in both. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hagar-and-slavery-vs-sarah-and-freedom
- **v. 25:** Chrysostom: "Hagar" was the local word for Sinai. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
  - Calvin rejects that explanation, along with Jerome's. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom41.iii.vi.iv.html
  - Coffman notes that scholars cannot trace Chrysostom's source. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/galatians-4.html
- **v. 25 ("present-day Jerusalem"):** TGC: refers to all who put the Mosaic Law at the center of how they relate to God and others. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/galatians/
- **v. 26:**
  - Matthew Henry: the Jerusalem above is the Christian state under the new covenant, open to Jews and Gentiles who believe. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-24.html
  - Piper: our lives are already written in that city's citizen register, and Sarah stands for it because her son came by God's act. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hagar-and-slavery-vs-sarah-and-freedom
- **v. 27:**
  - Guzik: the new covenant would soon have many more followers than the old. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
  - Luther: unbelievers have always predicted the Church's death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
  - TGC: the barren Sarah now has more children than Hagar. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/galatians/
- **v. 28:** Ellicott: the better reading is "ye" (you), meaning children born as the fulfilment of the promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
- **v. 29:**
  - Ellicott: Genesis 21:9 says "mocking". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - Barclay: the children of law now persecute the children of grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-24.html
- **v. 30 (how to apply "expel"):**
  - Guzik: law and grace cannot live together as principles of the Christian life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
  - Gangel (quoted by Precept Austin) reads it as a command to remove the legalisers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-4-commentary
  - Luther applies it to the Ishmaelites, the papists, and all others who trust in their own merits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mlg/galatians-4.html
  - Ellicott: A bold declaration of the incompatibility of Judaism with Christianity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
  - Guzik's devotional adds that God did not hate Ishmael and blessed him. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/isaac-and-ishmael/
- **v. 31:** Ellicott: the main point is that freedom is the essential character of the Church, and the verse belongs with 5:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/galatians/4.htm
